Over the past 5 years the share price has declined 36.3%, which raises the issue of whether the reset in expectations has gone far enough when measured against Salesforce's profit stream.

Recent moves into Super Intelligence export packages, government focused solutions and AI powered customer experience tools may support different assumptions about future earnings quality, capital needs and the durability of cash generation.

Does Salesforce Look Undervalued on Earnings?

The P/E ratio works well for Salesforce because earnings have become a key anchor for how the market frames the business today. In that lens, the stock trades on about 15.8x earnings, which is well below the Software sector average of roughly 30.7x and also beneath the broader peer group closer to 40.9x.

Because the current P/E sits below the level implied by a more tailored fair multiple that factors in Salesforce's own growth profile, profitability and risk, the shares screen as undervalued on this metric. Despite recent worries about AI competition and software outages weighing on sentiment, the market is still pricing Salesforce at a noticeable discount to where this earnings based model would usually place a large, established software platform. Salesforce (CRM) stock fell 25.4% in the month to November 23, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 5.0%. Its highest close of the past year was $264.42, on December 29, 2025. The shares closed at $185.46 on November 23. If Salesforce keeps growing at a little below its recent pace, how close to that December high could its shares get in three years?

A 25.4% drop in one month leaves many Salesforce watchers waiting for the fall to end before they buy. The cash held back for that purchase can still work for you while you wait. The Trefis Income Solution owns 50 companies that have each paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row, and together they yield about 3 times what the S&P 500 pays. See the Income Solution.

Salesforce Shares Could Be Worth About Their December High

On these assumptions, a Salesforce share would be worth about $264.31 three years from now. That is 42.5% above today's price, or 12.5% a year before dividends. It is also just short of the December high.

Salesforce trades at 15.7 times its earnings for the twelve months to July 31, 2026. One quarter lifts those earnings. In the quarter to July 31, 2026, net profit was $3.53 billion, well above operating profit of $2.42 billion, because of a large gain outside the core business. In the three quarters before, net profit was below operating profit. So the 15.7 P/E makes the stock look cheaper than its business alone would, and the scenario's year-three earnings start from this same base. That P/E is far below its average of 44.0 at the last 12 fiscal quarter ends. Part of that average comes from 2023 and 2024, when margins were lower. The scenario lifts the P/E only partway back toward that average, as a Trefis assumption.

Most of the gain, 77.2% of it, comes from revenue growing 9.5% a year. That pace is 0.85 times the 11.2% growth Salesforce delivered in the twelve months to July 2026. Another 32.0% comes from the higher P/E, and a lower margin takes some of the gain back.

Salesforce's Slack And Platform Business Grew Fastest

In fiscal 2026, one segment grew far faster than the rest. Agentforce 360 Platform, Slack and Other raised its revenue 22.6% in the year to January 31, 2026. The largest segment, Agentforce Service, grew 8.4%. Each of the other five segments grew 8.5% or less, so most revenue still grows far more slowly.

On the fiscal Q2 2027 call on August 26, 2026, management credited Slack and Agentforce for the quarter's revenue growth. Agentforce, its AI product, had reached $1.5 billion of annual recurring revenue. The company also raised its fiscal 2027 revenue guide to $46.1 billion to $46.4 billion. The middle of that range works out to fiscal 2027 growth of 11.4%, above the scenario's 9.5% a year.

Salesforce's operating margin today, 21.5%, is above its 19.2% average for the twelve-month periods ended July 2023 to April 2026. So the scenario moves the year-three margin partway toward that average, to 20.8%. That lower margin takes back 9.2% of the gain. Revenue growth has also swung. It was 10.3% in the twelve months to July 2024, 8.3% a year later and 11.2% in the latest twelve months. Because the latest pace is well above the two years before it, the scenario assumes a slower 9.5%.

Owning the stock for three years would return nothing if revenue shrank 2.7% a year, against 11.2% growth in the latest twelve months. The operating margin could fall to 14.6%, from 21.5% today, with the same result. So could the P/E, to 12.4 from 15.7 today.

Salesforce is expected to report fiscal Q3 2027 results in December 2026, showing revenue against management's guide for the quarter. Until then, money set aside to buy Salesforce at a better price can earn something while it waits.

title: NOW's Subscription Growth: Will Strong Retention Sustain Momentum?
detail:
NOW's Subscription Growth: Will Strong Retention Sustain Momentum?
Subhasish Mukherjee
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 11:20 AM EST 3 min read
NOW
CRM
PEGA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

ServiceNow NOW is benefiting from strong subscription revenue growth and high customer retention, reinforcing the stability of its recurring revenue business. In the third quarter of 2026, subscription revenues rose 21% year over year to $3.99 billion (20.5% in constant currency), accounting for approximately 97% of total revenues. Its renewal rate remained strong at 98%, compared with 97% in the year-ago quarter.

Strong customer retention is also supporting deeper enterprise relationships and cross-selling opportunities. ServiceNow ended the quarter with 680 customers generating more than $5 million in annual contract value (ACV), up approximately 23% year over year. Moreover, 19 of its top 20 deals included six or more products, highlighting broader platform adoption and opportunities to expand customer spending.

The company's expanding backlog further strengthens revenue visibility. Remaining performance obligations (RPO) reached $29.7 billion, growing 22.5% year over year in constant currency, while current RPO increased 21% to $13.65 billion. ServiceNow expects full-year 2026 subscription revenues of $15.78-$15.79 billion, indicating 21% constant-currency growth.

However, fourth-quarter current RPO growth is expected to moderate to 18.5%, reflecting a higher mix of on-prem deals and exclusions related to termination-for-convenience (T4C) backlog. Additionally, AI deployment services shifted approximately 25 basis points of third-quarter subscription revenue growth to professional services revenues, with a 50-basis-point impact expected in the fourth quarter.

Nevertheless, strong retention, expanding enterprise adoption and substantial contracted backlog should sustain ServiceNow's recurring revenue growth despite near-term pressures.

Rivals Benefiting From the Trend

Salesforce CRM competes with ServiceNow in customer service automation and AI-driven enterprise workflows. In second-quarter fiscal 2027, Salesforce reported 12% year-over-year growth in subscription and support revenues to $10.82 billion, while current remaining performance obligations increased 14% in constant currency. Salesforce's expanding Agentforce adoption and growing recurring revenue base are intensifying competition for enterprise customers seeking integrated automation solutions.

Pegasystems PEGA competes with ServiceNow in workflow automation, customer engagement and AI-powered business process management. In third-quarter 2026, Pegasystems reported 20% year-over-year growth in Pega Cloud annual contract value (ACV), while total ACV increased 6%. Pegasystems' expanding cloud adoption, with Pega Cloud accounting for 59% of total ACV, strengthens its competitive position in enterprise automation and subscription-based software solutions.

ServiceNow's shares have declined 40.1% year to date, underperforming the Zacks Computers - IT Services industry's fall of 25.5%.

Software stocks had a rough month. The iShares Expanded Tech-Software fund fell 13.9% in the month to the Nov 23 close. The broader Technology Select Sector SPDR fund fell 11.4%. Both figures are price only, measured from the Oct 23 close.

This article asks whether the selling hit the slowest growers hardest. It did not. ServiceNow lost 42.3%, Atlassian lost 38.7% and Datadog lost 37.3%. Salesforce lost 25.4%. These are total returns, with dividends, over the same month.

The three that fell most are the faster growers. Over the last twelve months, ServiceNow's revenue grew about 1.9 times as fast as Salesforce's. Datadog's grew about 3.0 times as fast. Datadog's growth has not faded. Datadog's sales rose 35.2% in the three months to September, up from 28.4% a year before.

Salesforce still grows too. Its revenue rose 10.8% in the three months to July. Its free cash flow is the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment. That figure rose 21.3% in the latest twelve months, to $15.2 billion.

Salesforce lost 25.4% in one month, even with its free cash flow up 21.3% over its latest twelve months. If you count on your savings for income, a fall that fast in one stock is hard to sleep through. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

Did the selling track growth or profit?

We ranked each stock twice: once by its one-month return and once by its revenue growth over the last twelve months. Then we measured how closely the two rankings match. This score is called a rank correlation. A score near zero means no link at all.

Across 39 application software stocks, the score was -0.16. Across 24 systems software stocks, it was -0.11. Both are close to zero. Fast growers did not fall less than slow ones.

Profit told the same story. Operating margin is the share of sales left as profit after running costs. Its score against the month's return was 0.05 in application software. In systems software it was -0.09.

The extremes make the point. Palantir Technologies grew revenue 87.1% and fell 19.0%. Open Text grew revenue 0.14% and fell 17.7%. Their falls were close despite very different growth.

TD Cowen Cut Its Salesforce Target to $275 From $300. It Still Sees 48% Upside

TD Cowen Cut Its Salesforce Target to $275 From $300. It Still Sees 48% Upside ©Kohlerphoto from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

TD Cowen cut its Salesforce price target to $275 from $300 on Nov. 23 and kept its Buy rating, which still leaves 48% upside.

Salesforce is 30% below its 52-week closing high because investors worry that AI agents will replace the paid seats it sells, a fear that has also hit ServiceNow.

Analysts haven't cut their earnings estimates, and the stock trades at under 13x forward earnings, against a five-year average of 27x.

TD Cowen's $275 is a fair target that needs only about 15x expected earnings, but the Dec. 2 report has to show organic growth picking up from 6%.

Salesforce (CRM:NYSE) is 30% below its 52-week closing high, and TD Cowen cut its price target to $275 on Nov. 23. That's still 48% above the stock's $185.46 close that day.

ServiceNow (NOW:NYSE) sells AI agents into many of the same budgets, and it's down 44% in a year on a worry the two share: that agents replace the people whose seats both companies charge for.

Investors want proof of growth

On Aug. 26, Salesforce reported second-quarter revenue up 11% to $11.3 billion, but $456 million of that came from Informatica. Without it, revenue grew about 6%. CFO and COO Robin Washington said Salesforce is "on track for second-half organic revenue reacceleration."

RBC Capital Markets analyst Rishi Jaluria warned on the RiskReversal Pod that "the AI companies are going to try to destroy Salesforce entirely."

TIKR tracks 56 analysts on Salesforce. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Salesforce, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Salesforce's Analyst Ratings

TD Cowen still says Buy

TD Cowen's Derrick Wood cut his target to $275 from $300 on Nov. 23 and kept his Buy rating. The firm's checks showed little change since the second quarter, so it expects in-line results and guidance. It also thinks a clearer read on AI bookings may have to wait for the seasonally important fourth quarter.

Citi's Tyler Radke cut his target to $198 from $263 the same day and kept a Neutral rating. He said customer and partner checks point to sluggish core growth and few AI deployments in production. BTIG trimmed its target to $250 from $300 on Nov. 18. Salesforce shares still rose 2.68% on Nov. 23 as software stocks bounced, with ServiceNow up 4.69%.

TIKR tracks 56 analysts on Salesforce. As of Nov. 20, before Citi's cut, their average target had fallen to $286 from $331 a year earlier.
